stem.text: Transition elements have variable oxidation states and form complex ions.
State two other typical chemical properties of a transition element.

explanation.text: The syllabus lists four typical chemical properties of transition elements: variable oxidation states, catalytic behaviour, formation of complex ions and formation of coloured compounds. The question already gives two of them, so the answer is the other two: they act as catalysts and they form coloured compounds. The single mark needs both. Physical properties such as high melting point or high density are not chemical properties, so the MS ignores them.

reasoningChain: Recall the four typical chemical properties listed in the syllabus.
Remove the two the question already gives (variable oxidation states, complex ions).
State the remaining two: catalytic activity and coloured compounds.

inferredMistakes.text: Repeating one of the properties already given in the stem, such as variable oxidation states, which the MS ignores.
Giving a physical property such as high melting point or high density instead of a chemical property.

stem.text: Explain why transition elements have variable oxidation states.

points.text: the d and s sub-shells / orbitals are close / similar in energy
alternatives: electrons in d and s sub-shells / orbitals available for bonding

explanation.text: In a transition element the 3d and 4s sub-shells have similar energies. Removing (or sharing) one more electron therefore costs only a little more energy each time, so the element can lose different numbers of electrons from the 4s and 3d sub-shells and form ions in several oxidation states. The answer must name both the d and s sub-shells and the idea of similar energy; 'shells' instead of sub-shells or orbitals is not credited.

reasoningChain: Name the two sub-shells involved: 3d and 4s.
State that they are close in energy.
Link this to electrons from both sub-shells being available, so different numbers of electrons can be lost.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing 'the 3d and 4s shells' instead of sub-shells or orbitals.
Saying only that transition elements have many electrons or an incomplete d sub-shell, without the idea that the d and s energies are similar.

stem.text: An aqueous solution of chromium(III) ions, Cr<sup>3+</sup>, contains the [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> complex ion.
Complete Figure 1.1 to show the electronic configuration for Cr<sup>3+</sup>.

stem.caption: Figure 1.1
stem.alt: [Ar] followed by five empty boxes labelled 3d and one separate empty box labelled 4s, for the candidate to fill with arrows.

points.text: [Ar] 3d: single arrow in each of the first three 3d boxes, the other two 3d boxes empty; 4s box empty

markScheme.note: The MS answer is the completed electrons-in-boxes diagram; shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Electrons-in-boxes diagram for Cr3+: five 3d boxes, the first three each containing one upward arrow and the last two empty, and one empty 4s box.

explanation.text: Cr is [Ar] 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>. When a transition element forms an ion it loses its 4s electrons first, then 3d electrons. Cr<sup>3+</sup> loses the one 4s electron and two 3d electrons, leaving [Ar] 3d<sup>3</sup>. By Hund's rule the three d electrons go into separate boxes with parallel spins, so three 3d boxes each hold one arrow, two 3d boxes are empty and the 4s box is empty.

reasoningChain: Write the configuration of the Cr atom: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹.
Remove three electrons, the 4s electron first and then two 3d electrons: [Ar] 3d³.
Put one arrow in each of three 3d boxes (unpaired, parallel spins) and leave the 4s box empty.

inferredMistakes.text: Removing electrons from the 3d sub-shell before the 4s, giving [Ar] 3d² 4s¹.
Pairing the three d electrons in the same box instead of placing them singly in separate boxes.

stem.text: State the type of bonding that exists between H<sub>2</sub>O and Cr<sup>3+</sup> in [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>.

explanation.text: Each water molecule is a ligand: it donates a lone pair of electrons from its oxygen atom into a vacant orbital on Cr<sup>3+</sup>. A covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from the same atom is a dative (coordinate) bond.

reasoningChain: Identify H₂O as the ligand with a lone pair on O.
Both electrons of the bond come from O, so the bond is dative covalent (coordinate).

inferredMistakes.text: Answering 'ionic' or 'hydrogen bonding' because the metal is a positive ion and water is polar.

stem.text: Explain why transition elements form complex ions.

guidance: I partially filled d-orbital(s) are energy accessible.

alternatives: vacant (d) orbital(s) can form dative bonds with ligands
vacant (d) orbital(s) can accept a (lone) pair of electrons to form a dative bond

explanation.text: A complex forms when ligands donate lone pairs to a central metal ion. For that the metal ion needs empty orbitals of suitable energy to accept the pairs. Transition element ions have vacant d orbitals that are energetically accessible, so they can accept lone pairs and form dative bonds with ligands. The MS needs the words 'vacant' (or empty/unoccupied) and 'orbital'; 'partially filled' d orbitals or 'sub-shells/energy levels' are not enough.

reasoningChain: Recall that ligands donate lone pairs to the metal ion.
State that the metal ion has vacant d orbitals of accessible energy to accept those pairs and form dative bonds.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying the d orbitals are 'partially filled' instead of vacant/empty, which the MS ignores.
Referring to vacant 'sub-shells' or 'energy levels' instead of orbitals.

stem.text: [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> can be converted into the [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>(OH)<sub>3</sub>] complex.
Suggest a suitable reagent for this conversion. State the type of reaction.

points.text: NaOH / OH– and precipitation / ligand exchange / neutralisation / deprotonation / acid-base

explanation.text: Going from [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> to the neutral [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>(OH)<sub>3</sub>] means three H<sub>2</sub>O ligands each lose an H<sup>+</sup> and become OH<sup>–</sup>. A small amount of a base such as NaOH(aq) (or NH<sub>3</sub>(aq)) removes the protons. The product has no charge, so it comes out of solution as a green precipitate. The MS accepts several names for the change: precipitation, deprotonation, acid–base/neutralisation, or ligand exchange (H<sub>2</sub>O replaced by OH<sup>–</sup>). Both the reagent and a type of reaction are needed for the mark.

reasoningChain: Compare the two formulas: three H₂O ligands have become OH⁻ and the charge has gone from 3+ to 0.
Choose a base that removes H⁺: NaOH(aq) / OH⁻ (NH₃(aq) also accepted).
Name the reaction type, e.g. deprotonation/acid–base or precipitation.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving only the reagent or only the reaction type; the mark needs both.
Writing 'precipitate' (the product) instead of a type of reaction such as precipitation, which the MS ignores.

stem.text: [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>(OH)<sub>3</sub>] reacts with an excess of NH<sub>3</sub>(aq) to form [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>.
Complete the equation for this reaction. State the type of reaction.

explanation.text: In excess ammonia all six ligands on chromium are replaced by NH<sub>3</sub>, which dissolves the precipitate. Six NH<sub>3</sub> come in; three H<sub>2</sub>O and three OH<sup>–</sup> leave. Check the charges: the left side is neutral, and the right side has 3+ on the complex balanced by three OH<sup>–</sup>. Because one set of ligands is swapped for another, the reaction is ligand exchange (substitution).

reasoningChain: Six NH₃ ligands replace all six existing ligands.
The released ligands are 3H₂O and 3OH⁻; check atoms and charge balance.
Name the reaction: ligand exchange / substitution.

inferredMistakes.text: Showing the OH⁻ ligands leaving as water without balancing the hydrogen, or forgetting the 3OH⁻ so the charges do not balance.
Calling the reaction precipitation or acid–base, when here the precipitate dissolves because ligands are exchanged.

stem.text: [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>(OH)<sub>3</sub>] shows stereoisomerism.
Draw three-dimensional diagrams in Figure 1.2 to suggest the two stereoisomers of [Cr(H2O)3(OH)3].

stem.caption: Figure 1.2
stem.alt: Two boxes labelled isomer 1 and isomer 2. Each contains Cr with one vertical bond drawn above and one below it, for the candidate to complete as a three-dimensional octahedral structure.

guidance: CON use of O2H once only then apply ecf.
One isomer - two water & two OH ligands at 180°.
One isomer – all water & all OH ligands at 90°.
markScheme.note: The MS shows the two isomer structures as drawn diagrams; shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Two octahedral three-dimensional structures around Cr. Left: H2O at top and bottom, H2O and OH on dashed bonds behind, HO and OH on wedges in front. Right: H2O at top and OH at bottom, H2O and OH on dashed bonds behind, H2O and OH on wedges in front.

explanation.text: The complex is octahedral with three H<sub>2</sub>O and three OH<sup>–</sup> ligands (type MA<sub>3</sub>B<sub>3</sub>), which has two geometrical isomers. In one, the three ligands of each kind sit on three corners of one face of the octahedron, so every H<sub>2</sub>O is at 90° to every other H<sub>2</sub>O and the same for OH (the 'fac' isomer). In the other, each set of three runs around a meridian, so one pair of H<sub>2</sub>O and one pair of OH are opposite each other at 180° (the 'mer' isomer). The diagrams must be three-dimensional: two bonds in the plane of the paper, wedges and dashed bonds for the others, as in the MS figure.

reasoningChain: Recognise six ligands around Cr³⁺, so the shape is octahedral.
Draw the first isomer with all three H₂O mutually at 90° (and all three OH at 90°).
Draw the second isomer with one H₂O pair and one OH pair trans (180°).
Use wedge and dashed bonds and write the ligands with O bonded to Cr (H₂O, HO), not O₂H.

inferredMistakes.text: Drawing two structures that are the same isomer rotated, instead of two different arrangements.
Writing a hydroxide ligand as O₂H or drawing a flat (2D) structure without wedge and dashed bonds.

stem.text: An aqueous solution of iron(III) ions, Fe<sup>3+</sup>, contains the [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> complex ion. This solution is acidic in a similar way to an aqueous solution of Al<sup>3+</sup>.
Suggest why a solution of Fe<sup>3+</sup> is acidic. Include an equation in your answer.

guidance: A M1 one of the H2O ligands loses a H+.
A M1 H2O in the complex can donate a H+.
A other alternatives for M2 for example [Fe(H2O)6]3+ + H2O → [Fe(H2O)5OH]2+ + H3O+ .

points.text: M1 [Fe(H2O)6]3+ / Fe3+ weakens O–H bonds / polarises O–H bonds

explanation.text: The small, highly charged Fe<sup>3+</sup> ion pulls electron density from the oxygen of each water ligand, which in turn draws electrons away from the O–H bonds. The weakened, polarised O–H bond lets a ligand lose H<sup>+</sup> to the solvent, so the complex acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid: [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>OH]<sup>2+</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>. Charge is conserved: 3+ on the left, 2+ and 1+ on the right. This is the same reason [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> solutions are acidic.

reasoningChain: Explain the cause: the high charge density of Fe³⁺ polarises and weakens the O–H bonds in the water ligands.
State the result: a water ligand releases H⁺, so the complex is a proton donor.
Write the equation [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ → [Fe(H₂O)₅OH]²⁺ + H⁺ and check the charges balance.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing an equation in which the charge on the product complex is not reduced by one, e.g. [Fe(H₂O)₅OH]³⁺.
Saying Fe³⁺ itself releases H⁺, or that Fe³⁺ reacts with water to form Fe(OH)₃ only, without explaining that the O–H bonds of the ligands are weakened.

stem.text: An aqueous solution of iron(II) ions, Fe<sup>2+</sup>, contains the [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex ion. This solution is also acidic.
Predict how the pH of 1.00 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) differs from the pH of 1.00 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq). Explain your answer.

guidance: A Fe3+ is more acidic / Fe2+ is less acidic for ‘lower pH / higher pH”.

points.text: Fe3+ has lower pH / Fe2+ has a higher pH and Fe3+ has a higher charge / smaller radii / higher charge density (so easier to hydrolyse) BOTH ora

explanation.text: The acidity in (f)(i) comes from the metal ion polarising the O–H bonds of its water ligands. Fe<sup>2+</sup> has a lower charge and a larger radius than Fe<sup>3+</sup>, so its charge density is lower. It polarises the O–H bonds less, fewer H<sup>+</sup> ions are released at the same concentration, and the Fe<sup>2+</sup> solution has the higher pH. The single mark needs both the pH comparison and the reason.

reasoningChain: Compare the two ions: Fe³⁺ has higher charge and smaller radius, so higher charge density.
Higher charge density polarises the water ligands more, releasing more H⁺.
Conclude that Fe²⁺(aq) has the higher pH (is less acidic).

inferredMistakes.text: Getting the direction wrong: saying Fe²⁺ has the lower pH because a higher pH means more acidic.
Giving the pH comparison without any reason based on charge, radius or charge density.

stem.text: Suggest why solutions of silver(I) salts are colourless.

guidance: I d orbital is full for M1.
CON M2 no d-d splitting / no ΔE gap.
A M2 cannot absorb energy in the visible spectrum.

points.text: M1 (Ag+) d-subshell is full / complete or d10 or d-orbitals are full
M2 no d-d(*) transition or no d electrons promoted / excited [1] or cannot absorb light in the visible spectrum
(must imply promotion) ‘d’ can be qualified from M1 for M2

explanation.text: Transition metal compounds are coloured because, in a complex, the d orbitals split into two sets of different energy and an electron in the lower set absorbs visible light to jump to the upper set. Ag<sup>+</sup> is [Kr] 4d<sup>10</sup>: every d orbital already holds two electrons, so there is no space in the upper set for an electron to move into. No d–d transition can happen, no visible light is absorbed and the solution is colourless. The answer must say the d sub-shell (or all d orbitals) is full, not just 'the d orbital'.

reasoningChain: Work out the configuration of Ag⁺: [Kr] 4d¹⁰, so the d sub-shell is full.
With every d orbital full, no electron can be promoted from a lower to a higher d orbital.
So no visible light is absorbed and the solution is colourless.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying there is 'no d-d splitting' or 'no energy gap', which contradicts M2; the orbitals still split, but there is nowhere for an electron to go.
Writing 'the d orbital is full' (singular), which the MS ignores for M1.

stem.text: A mixture contains sodium ethanedioate, Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, ethanedioic acid dihydrate, H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>•2H<sub>2</sub>O, and an unreactive solid.
5.00 g of this mixture is dissolved in distilled water and made up to 500 cm3 in a volumetric flask to form solution A.
Two different titration experiments are carried out using A.
In the first experiment, 25.0 cm3 of A requires 21.80 cm3 of acidified 0.0250 mol dm–3 MnO4–(aq) to reach the end-point.
2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>  +  5C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>  +  16H<sup>+</sup>  →  2Mn<sup>2+</sup>  +  10CO<sub>2</sub>  +  8H<sub>2</sub>O
In the second experiment, 25.0 cm3 of A requires 13.60 cm3 of 0.150 mol dm–3 OH–(aq) to reach the end-point.
H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>  +  2OH<sup>–</sup>  →  C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>  +  2H<sub>2</sub>O
Calculate the percentage by mass of Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> in the mixture.
[Mr: Na2C2O4, 134.0]

guidance:
A route 1 via 500 cm3 in M3 & M4
moles C2O42– = 1.3625 × 10–3 × 20 = 0.02725
moles H2C2O4 = 1.02 × 10–3 × 20 = 0.0204
moles Na2C2O4 = 0.02725 – 0.0204 = 0.00685.
mass Na2C2O4 = 0.00685 × 134 = 0.9179 g

A route 2 in M4 & M3
moles C2O42– = 1.3625 × 10–3 × 20 = 0.02725
moles H2C2O4 = 1.02 × 10–3 × 20 = 0.0204
mass C2O42– = 0.02725 × 134 = 3.6515 g
moles H2C2O4 = 0.0204 × 134 = 2.7336 g.
(M3) mass Na2C2O4 = 3.6515 – 2.7336 = 0.9179 g.
A ecf M4 answer to calculated value × 20 × 134.

points.text:
moles H2C2O4 = ½ × 2.04 × 10–3 = 1.02 × 10–3 ecf (moles OH– x ½)
any two [1] all four [2]

M4 moles Na2C2O4 = 3.425 × 10–4 × 20 = 6.85 × 10–3 ecf (in 500 cm3 A)
mass Na2C2O4 = 6.85 × 10–3 × 134 = 0.9179 g [1]

explanation.text: The two titrations measure different things. MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> oxidises every C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> unit, whether it came from Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> or from H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, so the first titration gives the total ethanedioate. OH<sup>–</sup> only reacts with the acid H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, so the second titration gives the acid alone. The difference is the amount of Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Use the mole ratios from the equations: 5 C2O42– per 2 MnO4– (× 2.5) and 1 H2C2O4 per 2 OH– (× ½). Then scale from the 25.0 cm3 portion to the whole 500 cm3 (× 20), convert to mass with Mr = 134.0 and divide by the 5.00 g sample. The water of crystallisation in the acid does not affect the answer, because only moles of the acid are used, never its mass.

inferredMistakes.text: Taking the moles of C₂O₄²⁻ from the manganate titration as the moles of Na₂C₂O₄, without subtracting the acid found in the second titration.
Using the ratio 2 : 5 the wrong way round (× 0.4 instead of × 2.5), or forgetting the × ½ for the acid–base titration.
Forgetting to scale from 25.0 cm³ to 500 cm³ (× 20) before finding the mass.
